key_insight: Localized, data-driven adjustments to speech timing — identified via reverse-correlation on precisely controlled synthetic speech — can covertly improve intelligibility more effectively than global slowing, often without listeners noticing a pronounced slowdown.
problem_solved: Determines whether and how changing speech rate actually helps comprehension for listeners with language or hearing challenges, offering a precise alternative to crude global slowing.
method: Use controllable text-to-speech to generate stimuli with fine-grained timing manipulations.
Apply reverse-correlation / data-driven analysis to discover temporal windows where slowing boosts comprehension.
Validate adapted timing with listener experiments measuring objective intelligibility (e.g., word recognition) and perceptual detectability.
impact: Provides a practical strategy for TTS, hearing-assistive devices, and ASR robustness to improve real-world comprehension with minimal perceptual cost; informs ML models that optimize temporal features for human listeners.
visual_elements: Waveform/prosody comparison: baseline vs global slow vs targeted slow with highlighted temporal regions showing where timing was adjusted.
Bar/line chart of intelligibility scores: baseline, global slow, and data-driven targeted slow (with error bars).
Pipeline diagram of the reverse-correlation loop: synthetic stimuli → listener responses → temporal weighting → adapted TTS.
Application icons: hearing aid, non-native listener, and ASR, showing deployment contexts for the method.
paper_title: Covertly improving intelligibility with data-driven adaptations of speech timing
paper_authors: Paige Tuttösí, Angelica Lim, H. Henny Yeung, Yue Wang, Jean-Julien Aucouturier
